title: Kp; Electrode potentials and the SHE
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EQ04#t2 term and clue written for the game; RX04#t4 term and clue written for the game; EQ04#t1 term and clue written for the game; RX04#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EQ04#N.3a, RX04#N.4a, EQ04#N.7b, RX04#N.10a, EQ04#N.11, RX04#N.13.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Partial pressure
items.clue: What one gas in a mixture would exert on its own in the same volume.

items.label: Potential difference
items.clue: What is measured between two half-cells; one half-cell alone can never give a reading.

items.label: Mole fraction
items.clue: Amount of one gas divided by the total amount of all the gases; these values add up to 1.

items.label: Standard hydrogen electrode
items.clue: Reference half-cell with H₂ bubbling over platinum in H⁺(aq); assigned 0.00 V by definition.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 2.0 mol N₂, 6.0 mol H₂ and 2.0 mol NH₃. The total pressure is 200 kPa. What is the partial pressure of H₂?

options.text: 67 kPa
300 kPa
120 kPa
1200 kPa

questions.stem: Why is the standard electrode potential of the hydrogen half-cell, 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂(g), given as 0 V?

options.text: No oxidation or reduction occurs at the hydrogen electrode.
Its absolute potential has been measured directly and found to be zero.
It is assigned by convention as the reference for other half-cells.
The platinum electrode is inert, so no potential develops.

questions.explanation: Only potential differences can be measured, so one half-cell must be chosen as the reference and given a value. By convention it is the SHE, at 0 V.

questions.stem: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), with partial pressures in kPa. Which gives Kp and its units?

options.text: Kp = p(SO₃)² / (p(SO₂)² × p(O₂)); units kPa
Kp = [SO₃]² / ([SO₂]² × [O₂]); units kPa⁻¹
Kp = p(SO₃)² / (p(SO₂)² × p(O₂)); units kPa⁻¹
Kp = p(SO₂)² × p(O₂) / p(SO₃)²; units kPa

questions.explanation: Products over reactants with powers from the coefficients. kPa² ÷ kPa³ = kPa⁻¹.

questions.stem: Standard electrode potentials: Mg²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Mg(s), E° = −2.37 V · Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Zn(s), E° = −0.76 V · Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s), E° = +0.34 V · Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Ag(s), E° = +0.80 V. Which species is the strongest oxidising agent?

options.text: Mg²⁺(aq), as its E° value is the largest in size
Mg(s), as it is the species most readily oxidised
Ag⁺(aq), as its E° value is the most positive
Ag(s), as silver has the most positive E° value

questions.explanation: Ag⁺ (+0.80 V) accepts electrons most readily, so it is the strongest oxidising agent listed.

questions.stem: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g); the forward reaction is endothermic. The total pressure of an equilibrium mixture is doubled at constant temperature. Which is correct once equilibrium is re-established?

options.text: Kp increases, and the mole fraction of NO₂ increases.
Kp is unchanged, and the mole fraction of NO₂ decreases.
Kp is unchanged, and the mole fraction of NO₂ is unchanged.
Kp decreases, because the forward reaction is endothermic.

questions.explanation: Higher pressure favours fewer moles of gas: 1 mol N₂O₄ against 2 mol NO₂. The position shifts left; Kp stays the same.

questions.stem: A standard Pb²⁺/Pb half-cell is connected to a standard hydrogen electrode. The voltmeter reads 0.13 V. The lead electrode is the negative electrode. Which statement is correct?

options.text: E°(Pb²⁺/Pb) = +0.13 V, because the voltmeter reading gives the lead electrode's potential directly, sign included.
E°(Pb²⁺/Pb) = −0.13 V, which is the absolute potential of the lead electrode on its own.
E°(Pb²⁺/Pb) = −0.13 V; the reading is the difference from the hydrogen electrode, which is 0 V by convention.
No reaction happens at the hydrogen electrode, because its E° is 0 V.

questions.explanation: A single half-cell cannot be measured alone. The SHE is defined as 0 V, so the whole 0.13 V is assigned to lead; lead is oxidised (it supplies the electrons), so its E° is negative.
